readiness.mainReason: The deck is sound and well sourced, but its full-launch trigger of 5% (slide 10) sits below the 8% conversion the year-one revenue case rests on (slide 8), so what the client must require before committing to a full launch changes once the two figures are reconciled.
readiness.highestRiskIssue: The month-three full-launch gate of 5% (slide 10) is below the 8% conversion the 5,000 pound revenue case depends on (slide 8), and the deck never reconciles them.
readiness.whatCouldChangeIt: If the team shows 5% is a deliberate minimum floor and gives the revenue at each conversion level, or aligns the gate with the 8% target, readiness rises to Nearly ready.

dimensions.name: Client decision usefulness
dimensions.note: The decision, the answer and the first step are stated plainly and early.

dimensions.name: Problem framing
dimensions.note: Specific problem and success target present, what is out of scope is not stated explicitly.

dimensions.name: Storyline and pyramid logic
dimensions.note: The governing insight leads on slide 1 and the flow is unbroken, but several interior titles are labels so title-only reconstruction is weaker.

dimensions.name: Evidence quality
dimensions.note: Grant risk, base and benchmark are sourced, and the conversion figure is marked as an assumption to test.

dimensions.name: Analysis and insight
dimensions.note: Findings are interpreted, the single-tier versus three-tier choice is reasoned and each feeds the recommendation.

dimensions.name: Recommendation specificity
dimensions.note: Action, owner, timeframe and metric are all named.

dimensions.name: Feasibility and implementation
dimensions.note: Sized to one coordinator with a real pilot, but one dependency (the partner discount) is not named.

dimensions.name: Risks, assumptions and uncertainty
dimensions.note: Load-bearing assumptions and risks are stated and the soft launch tests them.

dimensions.name: Slide-level communication
dimensions.note: Slide 1 leads with the answer, but many interior titles are bare labels rather than assertions.

dimensions.name: Professionalism, tone and confidentiality
dimensions.note: Professional throughout, roles not names, certainty is appropriate.

strengths.point: The deck answers the client question in the title and opens with the decision, so a busy reader knows the recommendation immediately.
strengths.quote: Client E should launch a paid membership scheme, starting with a single tier in the autumn.

strengths.point: The case for diversifying is quantified and sourced, which gives the recommendation a defensible starting point.
strengths.quote: Project grants are 80% of Client E's income (2024 accounts) and each is single-year.

strengths.point: The load-bearing number is honestly flagged as an assumption to test rather than presented as fact.
strengths.quote: The 8% assumption is conservative against the 32% attendance rate and is the main thing to test.

strengths.point: The plan is specific with a named owner, a phased sequence and a pilot the current team can run.
strengths.quote: The Client E coordinator owns the launch.

findings.title: The full-launch gate of 5% is below the 8% conversion the revenue case depends on, and the two are never reconciled.
findings.principle: Decision consistency: the criterion you gate a decision on must match the case that justifies it.
findings.diagnosis: Slide 8 builds the year-one revenue of about 5,000 pounds on 8% of the mailing list joining. Slide 10 then sets the trigger for a full launch at clearing 5% in the soft launch. Nothing on the deck reconciles the two, so the gate authorizes scaling at a conversion the revenue case does not support.

evidence.quote: If 8% of the mailing list joins at 45 pounds, that is about 5,000 pounds in year one.
Month three: full launch if the soft launch clears 5%.

findings.why: This is the reason readiness is not Nearly ready: the client will plan around 5,000 pounds while the plan lets them commit to a full launch at a level that would deliver closer to 3,000 pounds, so the month-three go decision rests on a target the gate does not enforce.
findings.reflect: Is 5% a floor below which you would stop, or the level that makes the scheme worth scaling, and what revenue does each conversion level produce.
findings.fix: Reconcile the gate with the revenue case: either raise the trigger to the conversion the year-one target needs, or keep 5% as an explicit floor and show the revenue at 5% and at 8% so the client commits with the real number in view. Gate on the number that defines success.

findings.title: A promised member benefit, the local-partner discount, depends on partners agreeing and is not listed among the assumptions to test.
findings.principle: Feasibility: a promised benefit that depends on a third party is an assumption until the third party is secured.
findings.diagnosis: Slide 7 promises a discount with local partners as a core member benefit. The assumptions on slide 9 cover mailing-list accuracy and staff strain but not whether any partner has agreed the discount, and the soft launch does not test it.

evidence.quote: Priority booking, two members-only events a year and a discount with local partners.
We assume the mailing list is accurate and that members-only events do not strain staff.

findings.why: If no partner has agreed a discount at launch, the membership advertises a benefit it cannot deliver and erodes trust with the first cohort. The recommendation still holds, so this only strengthens an already-sound plan.
findings.reflect: Which local partners have agreed the discount, and what is the fallback benefit if none has by launch.
findings.fix: Add the partner discount to the assumptions on the risk slide and confirm at least one partner before the soft launch, or lead with benefits fully within Client E's control.

comments.problem: Several interior titles are bare topic labels ("The numbers", "What members get", "First steps").
comments.why: The answer is clear from slide 1, but a reader skimming the interior titles gets topics not takeaways.
comments.fix: Turn each interior title into the one-line takeaway of its slide.

comments.problem: Only gross revenue is shown ("about 5,000 pounds in year one") with no admin cost or net contribution.
comments.why: For an income-diversification decision the net matters, though the deck argues admin is low and uses existing capacity.
comments.fix: State the expected admin cost or the net so the 5,000 pounds is read correctly.

questionsForLead: Is the 5% full-launch gate a deliberate minimum floor, or should it match the 8% the revenue case assumes.
Have any local partners agreed the member discount, or is that still to be secured.
Does the 5,000 pounds year-one figure net off any admin or event cost, or is it gross.
How large is the funding gap from the two grants not renewing, so the board can judge whether 5,000 pounds is a material first step.

learningNote.lesson: Gate a decision on the number that defines success. When the business case rests on one conversion rate, that rate is the threshold to proceed, not a lower one.
learningNote.weakHabit: Setting a go/no-go trigger separately from the revenue case it is meant to protect, so the two drift apart.
learningNote.exercise: For the recommendation, write the single number the case depends on, then write the go-criterion beside it. If they differ, decide on purpose which one governs and put the reason on the slide.

notAssessed: Whether the comparator membership prices (40 to 60 pounds) are current or complete. Only the deck's citation was provided, not the underlying sources.
Whether Client E has confirmed any local-partner discount. The deck does not say.
The size of the funding gap from the two non-renewing grants, so whether 5,000 pounds is a material first step could not be judged.
Visual design, layout and charts. Only slide text was provided.
Intended audience and known constraints were left blank in the input, so feasibility is judged only against constraints the deck itself states.
